newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia govt imminent after weeks of deadlock.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia govt imminent after weeks of deadlock.

text.p: Slovenia's prime minister-designate Janez Drnovsek failed on Friday to woo the right into joining a new coalition government and was likely to form a leftist administration with a slim majority.
Drnovsek, leader of the centre-left Liberal Democrats, has been struggling for two weeks to set up a new government, Slovenia's third since independence from Yugoslavia in 1991.

He had hoped to persuade right-wing parties into forming a wide national unity coalition to help him push through necessary economic reforms to prepare Slovenia for European Union membership early next century.
Sources close to the Liberal Democrat Party said Drnovsek, Slovenia's prime minister for the past four years, would present his new government to parliament later on Friday.
An alliance of three right-wing parties won 44 seats in the 90-member parliament in an inconclusive general election on November 10.
The Liberal Democrats are backed by former communists, the leftist Desus party and three other deputies to give them 46 seats in parliament, a majority of one.
"It is already sure that the government will be formed with 46 votes only," a Liberal Democrat source told Reuters.
Drnovsek's office said the announcement of a government lineup was most likely sometime after 6 p.m. (1700 GMT), following a meeting of the Liberal Democrat council.
While Slovenia is the most economically advanced of the former Yugoslav republics, it faces tough decisions on reducing public spending and speeding up privatisation if it is to stay in the race.
Slovenians on average are among the most wealthy people among Europe's former communist states with gross domestic product per capita in 1995 at $9,348.
Credit rating agencies put the tiny Alpine republic just behind the Czech Republic and ahead of Poland.
But leaning on leftist parties for support could slow down Drnovsek's drive to boost the economy -- one of the reasons he sought backing from the alliance.
The alliance is made up of the conservative People's Party, the centre-right Social Democrats and Christian Democrats.
People's Party leader Marjan Podobnik said the differences between the Liberal Democrats and the right were too great and no agreement could be found to form a new government.

"At the last meeting today we found out that in spite of trying to set up a government of national unity, it is not possible," Podobnik told Slovenian radio. "The differences among the parties are too big."
Social Democrat leader Janez Jansa said Drnovsek faced problems ahead.
"The government with a minimal majority can make some decisions but not key strategic decisions," Jansa, a former defence minister, told state radio.
One stumbling block could be changes to the constitution to enable Slovenia to join the EU -- a parliamentary vote which would need a two-thirds majority.
